summary.text: The expectation operator is the E that stands for the expected value of a random variable X, written E(X), E[X] or EX.
Authors style the E in different ways, as upright, italic or blackboard bold, and use several kinds of brackets.
Other notations exist too: μ_X is popular, ⟨X⟩ is common in physics, and M(X) is used in Russian-language literature.

facts.label: Random vectors
facts.value: Taken component by component: E[X]_i = E[Xᵢ]

items.prompt: One textbook writes E[X], another writes EX, and a third writes E(X) for the same random variable. What is going on?

options.label: They are three different quantities
The brackets show how many outcomes there are
Each form is for a different kind of variable
They are different spellings of the same idea

items.explain: The bracket forms are all used for the same thing, the expected value of X.

items.prompt: A physics paper writes ⟨X⟩ for a measured quantity X. What is it most likely taking?

options.label: Its average, the expected value
Its largest possible value
Its smallest possible value
Its chance of occurring

items.explain: Physicists commonly use ⟨X⟩ for the expected value.

items.prompt: A German student sees the word Erwartungswert next to a letter E in a probability lecture. What does it name?

options.label: The spread of a random variable
The most likely single outcome
The expected value
The chance an event happens

items.explain: In German, E stands for Erwartungswert, meaning expected value.

items.prompt: A random vector holds two numbers, such as a person's height and weight. How is its expected value defined?

options.label: Each part gets its own expected value, one by one
The two numbers are added first, then averaged
Only the first number is ever averaged
It cannot be defined for more than one number

items.explain: The expected value of a random vector is taken component by component.

items.prompt: A random table of numbers is grid-shaped, with a random entry in each cell. How would you define its expected value?

options.label: Add every cell into a single total
Average only the cells along the top row
Keep the largest cell and drop the rest
Take the expected value of each cell on its own

items.explain: For a random matrix, each entry's expected value is taken separately to form a new matrix.

items.prompt: A Russian-language paper writes M(X). What does that most likely mean?

options.label: The most common value of X
The expected value of X
The maximum value of X
The middle value of X when sorted

items.explain: M(X) is the notation for expected value in Russian-language literature.

paragraphs.heading: The letter E
paragraphs.text: The expected value of a random variable, also called its expectation or mean, is a generalization of the weighted average. The expectation operator is the letter E placed in front of a random variable X to stand for that value. It is usually written E(X), E[X] or EX.

paragraphs.heading: Styles and brackets
paragraphs.text: Writers style the letter in several ways: an upright E, an italic E, or a blackboard bold 𝔼, and ℰ also turns up. The brackets vary as well. E(X), E[X] and EX are all in common use.

paragraphs.heading: Other notations
paragraphs.text: The letter E is not the only choice. μ_X is another popular way to write the expected value. In physics, ⟨X⟩, ⟨X⟩_av and X̄ are common. Russian-language writing uses M(X) instead.

paragraphs.heading: Where the E fits
paragraphs.text: The idea has also been called mathematical hope, described as the sum hoped for multiplied by the chance of getting it. The E symbol later became popular with English writers. In other languages the letter has its own meaning: German readers take E for Erwartungswert, Spanish ones for esperanza matemática, and French ones for espérance mathématique.

paragraphs.heading: What the operator computes
paragraphs.text: Suppose X has possible outcomes x₁,..., xₖ with probabilities p₁,..., pₖ. Then the operator gives E [X] = x₁p₁ + x₂p₂ + ⋯ + xₖpₖ. Because the probabilities add up to 1, this reads as a weighted average of the outcomes. When it is finite, the result can be read as the long-run average of independent repeats of the same random experiment. In the most general setting, the operator is a Lebesgue integral of the variable, taken with respect to the underlying probability measure.

paragraphs.heading: Vectors and matrices
paragraphs.text: The operator also works on a random vector, which is a random variable with several dimensions. It acts one component at a time, so E[X]_i = E[Xᵢ]. A random matrix is treated in the same way, with E[X]_ij = E[X_ij].
